title: Coulomb's law & electric fields
examples: How does the distance between two charges affect the force?
What is the difference between electric force and electric field strength?
Can you show me how to calculate the field strength at a specific point?

explain.say: Today we study the force between charges. The force is given by the formula k times q one times q two divided by r squared.
The constant k is a number that depends on the medium. In a vacuum, k is approximately nine times ten to the nine newtons meter squared per coulomb squared.
Next we look at electric field lines. These lines show the direction of the force. Positive charges point lines away from them.
The electric field strength E is the force F on a small positive test charge q. The formula is E equals F divided by q.
For example, if you place a positive charge near a negative charge, the field lines will curve from positive to negative.
In everyday life, think about static electricity on a balloon. Rubbing it against your hair gives it a charge and creates an electric field.

faq.q: What is the difference between force and field strength?
faq.a: Force is the actual push or pull between two objects. Field strength is the force per unit charge at a specific point.
asks: Is E the same as F?
How do I calculate field strength?
What is the unit for E?

faq.q: Does the distance matter for the force?
faq.a: Yes, the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance. If you double the distance, the force becomes four times weaker.
asks: How fast does force drop with distance?
Does the square root apply here?

faq.q: What do the field lines tell me?
faq.a: Field lines show the direction of the electric force at every point. They start on positive charges and end on negative charges.
asks: Are field lines like magnetic field lines?
Do field lines show strength too?

faq.q: Can I use this for magnets too?
faq.a: The concept is very similar to magnetism. Both use field lines to map invisible forces. However, the underlying physics equations differ.
asks: Are the rules the same for magnets?
What's the connection between E and B?

faq.a: A test charge is a very small, positive hypothetical charge used only for calculation. It helps us measure the field strength at a point.
asks: Do I need a test charge for every problem?
What is the purpose of qtest?
Is the test charge itself affected?

facts: The electric force between two point charges is given by F equals k q₁ q₂ divided by r squared.
Electric field strength E is defined as the electric force F divided by the test charge q.
Field lines are denser where the electric field strength is stronger.
Like charges repel each other, and unlike charges attract each other.

quiz.say: A point charge creates an electric field strength at a distance r. This strength is proportional to:

options.show: The charge divided by the distance.
options.say: The charge divided by the distance.

options.show: The distance squared divided by the charge.
options.say: The distance squared divided by the charge.

options.show: The charge divided by the distance squared.
options.say: The charge divided by the distance squared.

options.show: The charge squared divided by the distance.
options.say: The charge squared divided by the distance.

quiz.why: Field strength E is calculated by dividing the force F by the test charge q. Since F is proportional to q/r², E becomes proportional to 1/r².

wrong.0: This forgets the square relationship with the distance, making the force seem too strong.
wrong.1: This reverses the relationship completely, suggesting distance increases strength.
wrong.3: This incorrectly squares the charge, which is not part of the field strength calculation.

quiz.say: If you move away from a charge, how does the electric field strength change?

options.show: The field strength decreases by the square of the distance increase.
options.say: The field strength decreases by the square of the distance increase.

options.show: It stays the same regardless of distance.
options.say: It stays the same regardless of distance.

options.show: It increases as you move away.
options.say: It increases as you move away.

quiz.why: Because E is proportional to one over r squared, moving further away causes a rapid drop in field strength.

wrong.1: This suggests a simple straight-line decrease, ignoring the inverse square nature of the force.
wrong.2: This would mean the charge has no effect on the field strength at all.
wrong.3: This contradicts the fundamental nature of field lines spreading out from a source.

quiz.say: Which statement correctly describes the direction of electric field lines?

options.show: They always point from negative to positive.
options.say: They always point from negative to positive.

options.show: Their direction depends on the observer's angle.
options.say: Their direction depends on the observer's angle.

options.show: They point away from positive charges and towards negative charges.
options.say: They point away from positive charges and towards negative charges.

options.show: They always point in a straight line.
options.say: They always point in a straight line.

quiz.why: This describes the fundamental rule of electric field lines, showing the direction of the net force.

wrong.0: This reverses the established convention for field line direction.
wrong.1: The direction of the field at a point is fixed by the charges present.
wrong.3: Field lines curve when charges are arranged in complex patterns.
